---
title: "Component 2 — Run Expectancy, Win Probability, Leverage and WPA"
---

## The situational layer

Component 1 gave us game state. This component turns state into **meaning**: how
much a moment is worth, and how much a play changed the game. Nothing here is
imported from another league — the run-expectancy matrix and the win-probability
model are both estimated from this season.

## Run Expectancy

$RE(\text{base state}, \text{outs})$ is the average number of runs a team scores
from that state to the end of the half-inning. It is the basis of Expected Runs
Added:

$$RE24 = RE_{\text{after}} - RE_{\text{before}} + \text{runs scored}$$

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-re
#| eval: false
source("../R/R02_wpa_leverage.R")

re_tbl <- fit_run_expectancy(pbp)
run_expectancy_table(re_tbl)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-re
#| eval: false
from components import c02_wpa_leverage as c02

re_model = c02.fit_run_expectancy(pbp)
c02.run_expectancy_table(re_model)
```

:::

| bases | 0 outs | 1 out | 2 outs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `___` | 0.584 | 0.319 | 0.122 |
| `1__` | 0.939 | 0.537 | 0.221 |
| `_2_` | 1.192 | 0.834 | 0.391 |
| `12_` | 1.547 | 1.115 | 0.440 |
| `__3` | 1.135 | 0.937 | 0.551 |
| `1_3` | 1.874 | 1.427 | 0.620 |
| `_23` | 1.889 | 1.550 | 0.537 |
| `123` | 2.070 | 1.789 | 0.760 |

The matrix is strictly decreasing in outs for all eight base states — the
invariant any correct RE table must satisfy, and one the test suite checks.

## Win Probability

::: {.callout-note}
## Why a model and not a lookup

With 250 games, an (inning × base-out × score-margin) grid cannot be filled by
counting. A lookup produces jagged, non-monotonic probabilities that look broken
on a scoreboard. A logistic model with well-chosen features stays smooth and
monotonic, which is what a fan-facing number has to be.
:::

Features and the reasoning behind each:

| feature | why it is there |
|---|---|
| `score_diff` | the value of a lead |
| `innings_left` | how much time remains to change it |
| `score_diff × innings_left` | a lead is worth more as innings run out |
| `re_state` | the run potential of the current base-out state |
| `is_bottom` | the home team bats last |

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-wp
#| eval: false
wp_model <- fit_win_probability(pbp, re_tbl)
wp_metrics(wp_model, pbp, re_tbl)
```

R uses `glm()` with a binomial family — the idiomatic choice, and identical in
form to the hand-rolled gradient descent used on the Python side.

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-wp
#| eval: false
wp_model = c02.fit_win_probability(pbp, re_model)
c02.wp_metrics(wp_model)
```

:::

| metric | value |
|---|---|
| plate appearances | 18,834 |
| accuracy | 0.774 |
| Brier score | 0.144 |
| log loss | 0.433 |
| base rate | 0.517 |

## Win Probability Added

$$WPA = WP_{\text{after}} - WP_{\text{before}}$$

The subtlety is the **half-inning flip**: after the third out the other team
bats, so "the batting team" changes. When the sides change, the batting team's
win probability becomes the *complement* of the next state's.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-wpa
#| eval: false
pbp <- add_wpa(pbp, wp_model, re_tbl)
biggest_swings(pbp, n = 8)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-wpa
#| eval: false
enriched = c02.add_win_probability(pbp, wp_model, re_model)
c02.biggest_swings(enriched, n=8)
```

:::

The largest swings of the season are exactly what a human would pick:

| inning | half | outcome | wp before | wp after | WPA |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11 | Bottom | home run | 0.144 | 0.970 | **+0.826** |
| 9 | Bottom | out | 0.711 | 0.000 | **−0.711** |
| 10 | Bottom | home run | 0.162 | 1.000 | **+0.838** |

Walk-off home runs and game-ending outs — the model found them without being
told what a walk-off is.

## Leverage Index

Leverage answers *how much can the game move from here?* Following the standard
definition, it is the expected absolute win-probability swing from a state,
normalized so an average plate appearance equals 1.0:

$$LI(\text{state}) = \frac{E\left[\,|\Delta WP|\ \middle|\ \text{state}\right]}{E\left[\,|\Delta WP|\,\right]}$$

We enumerate the plausible outcomes of a plate appearance with their league
frequencies, apply each to the state with a small transition model, and average
the resulting $|\Delta WP|$.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-li
#| eval: false
pbp <- add_leverage(pbp, wp_model, re_tbl)
leverage_profile(pbp)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-li
#| eval: false
enriched, li = c02.add_leverage(enriched, wp_model, re_model)
c02.leverage_profile(enriched)
```

:::

| statistic | value |
|---|---|
| mean | **1.000** |
| median | 0.889 |
| p90 | 2.010 |
| p95 | 2.620 |
| max | 8.230 |
| share above 2.0 | 0.102 |

The mean of exactly 1.000 is by construction; the useful check is the shape —
about 10 % of plate appearances are genuine high-leverage moments, and the
maximum of 8.2 is in the right range for real baseball.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Performance

Leverage needs one win-probability evaluation per possible outcome per plate
appearance — roughly 113,000 model calls for a season. Evaluated row by row this
took minutes; vectorized it takes about five seconds, which is what makes the
metric usable on a live feed rather than only in post-processing.
:::

## Game flow

The single most valuable storytelling graphic in baseball: where a game was won
and lost.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-flow
#| eval: false
flow <- game_flow(pbp, "y1_d122_IOL_VAS")
plot_game_flow(flow, home_team = "VAS", away_team = "IOL")
```
